question: When two-way traffic must share one lane for a limited distance, what coordination rule and control methods apply?
model_answer: Direct Answer: When traffic in both directions must use a single lane for a limited distance, the MUTCD requires that movements from each end be coordinated, except that on short work spaces on low-volume roads with full mutual visibility the movement may be self-regulating. Permitted control methods include flaggers (one or two, depending on visibility), temporary traffic control signals, and — as explanatory cross-reference — the techniques described in Section 6E.01 for two-lane highway work. Standards (mandatory): - "Except as provided in Paragraph 4 of this Section, when traffic in both directions must use a single lane for a limited distance, movements from each end shall be coordinated." - For the related situation of two-lane, two-way traffic on one roadway of a normally-divided highway: "opposing vehicular traffic shall be separated with either temporary traffic barriers (concrete safety-shape or approved alternate), channelizing devices, Narrow Two-Way Traffic (W6-4) signs on flexible supports (see Section 6H.17), or a temporary raised island throughout the length of the two-way operation. The use of markings and complementary signing, by themselves, shall not be used." Options (permitted): - When a one-lane, two-way TTC zone is short enough for a flagger to see from one end of the zone to the other, traffic may be controlled by either a single flagger or by a flagger at each end of the section. - If the work space on a low-volume street or road is short and road users from both directions can see traffic approaching from the opposite direction through and beyond the worksite, the movement through the one-lane, two-way constriction may be self-regulating. - Traffic control signals may be used to control vehicular traffic movements in one-lane, two-way TTC zones (see Figure 6P-12 and Chapter 4O). Support (informational): - Techniques for controlling vehicular traffic under one-lane, two-way conditions are described in Section 6E.01. Visual evidence: - [Image 1] Figure 6P-12 (Typical Application 12) illustrates a one-lane, two-way operation controlled by temporary traffic control signals, with W3-3 signal-ahead warning signs, R10-6 STOP HERE ON RED signs, temporary markings, and tapered channelizing devices at each end. - [Image 2] Figure 6P-14 (Typical Application 14, Haul Road Crossing) shows the same one-lane, two-way constriction controlled two alternative ways: "A – Using temporary traffic control signals" (W3-3, R10-6) and "B – Using flaggers" (W20-7 flagger symbol sign and a flagger station 30 ft in advance), demonstrating the permitted control methods. - [Image 3] The full page view of Chapter 6E shows Section 6E.01 (coordination Standard and self-regulating Option), Section 6E.02 (Flagger Method), Section 6E.03 (Flag Transfer Method), and Section 6E.04 (Pilot Car Method) as the family of control methods for one-lane, two-way operation. - [Image 5] The full page view of Figure 6L-1 illustrates use of a STOP/SLOW Automated Flagger Assistance Device (AFAD) with gates, R1-1/W20-8 STOP/SLOW signs, and WAIT ON STOP / GO ON SLOW plaques at each end of a one-lane, two-way section, showing another way flagger-based control can be implemented. Citations: - Section 6E.01 Standard §1 (p.787) - Section 6E.01 Option §4 (p.787) - Section 6E.02 Option §2 (p.787) - Section 6E.05 Option §1 (p.788) - Section 6N.14 Standard §2 (p.850) - Section 6N.09 Support §6 (p.846) - Figure 6P-12 (p.883) - Figure 6P-14 (p.887) - Page 828 - Page 868
gold_answer: Movements from both ends must be coordinated, except for a short, low-volume, mutually visible work zone that can self-regulate. Methods include flaggers, flag transfer, a pilot car, temporary traffic signals, or stop/yield control.
